CourseName: CEN3722 - Introduction to Human Computer Interfaces

Outcomes.Text: Explain Nielsen's ten usability heuristics and the design rationale behind each principle.
Identify usability violations in a user interface by applying Nielsen's heuristics systematically.
Apply a structured heuristic evaluation process to independently assess peer prototypes.
Evaluate the severity of usability problems using a standardized severity rating scale.
Analyze and aggregate findings across multiple evaluators to produce a consolidated list of usability issues.
Create formal heuristic evaluation reports that document violations, severity ratings, and design recommendations.

Topics.Title: Introduction to Heuristic Evaluation
Topics.Summary: Heuristic Evaluation (HE) is a structured usability inspection method in which evaluators examine an interface against a set of recognized usability principles. This topic introduces the method's purpose, origins, and key advantages over other evaluation approaches.

Elements.Title: What Is Heuristic Evaluation?
Elements.BodyText: Heuristic Evaluation is a discount usability engineering method that allows experts to identify usability problems in a user interface design without the need for live user testing.
Elements.Notes: Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich introduced HE in the early 1990s as a cost-effective alternative to full user studies. It is considered a 'discount' method because it requires fewer resources while still uncovering a significant proportion of usability issues.

Items.Text: HE is an inspection method, not a user test — evaluators act as surrogates for end users.
It is most effective when conducted by usability specialists rather than novice reviewers.
The method can be applied at any stage of the design process, including early prototypes.
HE is particularly valued for its speed and relatively low cost compared to lab-based testing.

Elements.Title: Origins and Context
Elements.BodyText: Nielsen and Molich developed the heuristic evaluation method in 1990, later refining the set of heuristics to the ten canonical principles that are widely used today.
Elements.Notes: The original set of heuristics was derived from factor analysis of 249 usability problems. The refined list of ten heuristics published by Nielsen in 1994 remains the industry standard.

Items.Text: The ten heuristics were empirically derived from analysis of real usability problems.
Nielsen's 1994 refinement consolidated earlier, broader lists into ten actionable principles.
The heuristics are intentionally high-level so they apply across diverse interface types.

Elements.Title: When to Use Heuristic Evaluation
Elements.BodyText: HE is appropriate at multiple points in the design lifecycle, from sketches and wireframes through high-fidelity prototypes and live products.
Elements.Notes: Evaluating early-stage prototypes helps teams catch fundamental structural issues before costly development. Evaluating a live product can benchmark quality and prioritize redesign efforts.

Items.Text: Early-stage evaluation catches conceptual and navigation issues before development begins.
Mid-fidelity evaluations surface interaction and feedback problems in interactive prototypes.
Post-launch evaluations identify persistent issues and inform iterative improvement cycles.
HE complements rather than replaces user testing — both methods surface different classes of issues.

Elements.Title: Advantages and Limitations
Elements.BodyText: HE offers speed, low cost, and the ability to evaluate interfaces without recruiting participants, but it also carries inherent limitations related to evaluator expertise and coverage.
Elements.Notes: Studies show that a single evaluator finds only about 35% of usability problems; five evaluators together typically find around 75%. This motivates the multi-evaluator approach required in this module.

Items.Text: A major advantage is that HE does not require access to real end users.
Evaluator expertise directly affects the quality and breadth of findings.
HE can miss usability problems that only emerge during authentic user tasks.
Using multiple evaluators significantly increases problem discovery rates.

Topics.Title: Nielsen's Ten Usability Heuristics
Topics.Summary: This topic covers each of Nielsen's ten heuristics in detail, explaining their meaning, rationale, and common interface violations. Mastery of these principles is the foundation for conducting a valid heuristic evaluation.

Elements.Title: Heuristic 1 — Visibility of System Status
Elements.BodyText: The system should always keep users informed about what is going on through appropriate feedback within reasonable time.
Elements.Notes: Examples include progress bars during file uploads, loading spinners, highlighted active menu items, and confirmation messages after form submission. Violations include pages that appear frozen after a user action with no indication of processing.

Items.Text: Users should never wonder whether their action was registered by the system.
Feedback must be timely — delays greater than one second require a visible indicator.
Status messages should be meaningful and located where the user's attention is focused.

Elements.Title: Heuristic 2 — Match Between System and the Real World
Elements.BodyText: The system should speak the users' language, using words, phrases, and concepts familiar to the user rather than system-oriented terminology.
Elements.Notes: The 'desktop metaphor' in operating systems is a classic example of matching the real world — files, folders, trash. Violations include using database field names as form labels or displaying error codes instead of plain-language messages.

Items.Text: Interface language should reflect the vocabulary of the target user group, not developers.
Icons and metaphors should map naturally to their real-world counterparts.
Information should appear in a natural and logical order that reflects users' mental models.

Elements.Title: Heuristic 3 — User Control and Freedom
Elements.BodyText: Users often choose system functions by mistake and need a clearly marked 'emergency exit' to leave the unwanted state without having to go through an extended dialogue.
Elements.Notes: Undo and redo are the canonical examples. Violations include multi-step processes with no way to go back, or dialogs that have no cancel button. Supporting freedom reduces fear of exploration.

Items.Text: Undo and redo functions are essential implementations of this heuristic.
Destructive actions should be reversible or require explicit confirmation before execution.
Users should be able to cancel any multi-step process at any point without side effects.

Elements.Title: Heuristic 4 — Consistency and Standards
Elements.BodyText: Users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations, or actions mean the same thing. Follow platform and industry conventions consistently.
Elements.Notes: Internal consistency means the same action always produces the same result within an application. External consistency means following established platform conventions (e.g., blue underlined text for links). Violations include using 'Submit,' 'Send,' and 'Go' interchangeably for the same action type.

Items.Text: Internal consistency requires that identical actions produce identical outcomes throughout the interface.
External consistency aligns the interface with platform-wide or industry-wide conventions.
Inconsistent terminology forces users to expend cognitive effort resolving ambiguity.

Elements.Title: Heuristic 5 — Error Prevention
Elements.BodyText: Even better than good error messages is a careful design that prevents problems from occurring in the first place.
Elements.Notes: Examples include disabling buttons that are not currently applicable, using date pickers instead of free-text date fields, and providing inline format hints before submission. This heuristic is considered more valuable than error recovery because it eliminates the problem entirely.

Items.Text: Constrain user input to valid options wherever possible to eliminate entry errors.
Warn users before they commit to potentially destructive or irreversible actions.
Design workflows that make errors difficult to make rather than easy to recover from.

Elements.Title: Heuristic 6 — Recognition Over Recall
Elements.BodyText: Minimize the user's memory load by making objects, actions, and options visible; the user should not have to remember information from one part of the dialogue to another.
Elements.Notes: Menus, toolbars, and autocomplete are all recognition-based mechanisms. Command-line interfaces are recall-based and place a higher cognitive burden on users. Breadcrumbs help users recognize where they are without having to recall their navigation path.

Items.Text: Visible options reduce cognitive load by allowing users to recognize rather than recall choices.
Instructions and relevant information should be visible or easily retrievable at the point of use.
Minimizing the need to transfer information mentally between interface sections reduces errors.

Elements.Title: Heuristic 7 — Flexibility and Efficiency of Use
Elements.BodyText: Accelerators — unseen by novice users — may often speed up interaction for expert users so that the system can cater to both inexperienced and experienced users.
Elements.Notes: Keyboard shortcuts, macros, customizable toolbars, and type-ahead search are common examples. Violations include interfaces that force all users through the same lengthy workflow regardless of experience level.

Items.Text: Novice and expert users have different interaction needs that the interface should accommodate.
Keyboard shortcuts and hotkeys allow experts to bypass menu-driven navigation.
Personalization features let users tailor frequently used functions for faster access.

Elements.Title: Heuristic 8 — Aesthetic and Minimalist Design
Elements.BodyText: Dialogues should not contain irrelevant or rarely needed information, as every extra unit of information competes with and diminishes the relative visibility of relevant information.
Elements.Notes: This heuristic does not mean interfaces must be visually plain — it means every element should earn its place. Violations include dashboard pages cluttered with metrics the primary user never needs, or help text that appears for options the user did not select.

Items.Text: Each interface element should serve a clear purpose for the primary user task.
Extraneous content reduces the signal-to-noise ratio and increases cognitive load.
Visual hierarchy should direct user attention toward the most critical information first.

Elements.Title: Heuristic 9 — Help Users Recognize, Diagnose, and Recover from Errors
Elements.BodyText: Error messages should be expressed in plain language, precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution.
Elements.Notes: A violation is displaying only an HTTP status code (e.g., '404') with no explanation or guidance. A good error message tells the user what happened, why, and what they can do next. Avoid blaming the user in error message language.

Items.Text: Error messages must use plain language that the target user can understand.
Messages should clearly identify the specific problem rather than generic failure notices.
Every error message should include a constructive path forward or suggested remedy.

Elements.Title: Heuristic 10 — Help and Documentation
Elements.BodyText: Even though it is better if the system can be used without documentation, it may be necessary to provide help; such information should be easy to search and focused on the user's task.
Elements.Notes: Good help systems are searchable, task-oriented, and concise. Violations include documentation that is only accessible from the home page, or help content written in technical jargon. Context-sensitive help that appears relevant to the user's current task is the gold standard.

Items.Text: Help documentation should be easy to find at the moment of need, not buried in menus.
Content should be organized around user tasks rather than system features or components.
Concise, step-by-step guidance is more effective than lengthy conceptual descriptions.

Topics.Title: The Heuristic Evaluation Process
Topics.Summary: Conducting a valid heuristic evaluation requires following a structured process that goes beyond simply reading the heuristics. This topic outlines the key phases of an HE, from preparation through individual evaluation to finding consolidation.

Elements.Title: Preparing for the Evaluation
Elements.BodyText: Before beginning an evaluation, evaluators must understand the system's intended users, primary use cases, and scope of the interface to be reviewed.
Elements.Notes: Without context about target users and tasks, evaluators cannot accurately judge whether a violation is minor or critical. A one-page briefing document or scenario description is typically sufficient preparation.

Items.Text: Evaluators should review any available personas or user profiles before starting.
Define which interface sections or user flows are in scope for the current evaluation.
Establish representative tasks or scenarios that guide the walkthrough of the interface.
Agree on the version of the prototype to be evaluated so all evaluators review the same artifact.

Elements.Title: Conducting the Individual Evaluation
Elements.BodyText: Each evaluator independently inspects the interface, walking through it multiple times and noting any elements that violate one or more of the ten heuristics.
Elements.Notes: Independence is critical — evaluators must not collaborate or share findings during this phase. Typically, evaluators traverse the interface at least twice: once to get a feel for the overall interaction flow, and once to focus on specific elements against each heuristic.

Items.Text: Evaluators must work independently to prevent anchoring bias from influencing findings.
A minimum of two walkthroughs is recommended — one holistic, one heuristic-focused.
Every identified problem should be documented with a reference to the heuristic it violates.
Note the specific location of each violation so it can be reproduced and verified.

Elements.Title: Documenting Usability Problems
Elements.BodyText: Each usability problem must be recorded with enough detail that someone unfamiliar with the evaluation can locate and understand the issue.
Elements.Notes: A well-formed problem report includes: the location in the interface, a description of the violation, the heuristic(s) violated, and a suggested fix. Screenshots or annotated images significantly improve the clarity of reports.

Items.Text: Each finding should reference the exact screen, component, or interaction step where it occurs.
The problem description should explain what the violation is, not just that a violation exists.
Naming the specific heuristic violated provides a principled basis for the finding.
Including a recommended fix increases the actionability of the evaluation report.

Elements.Title: Number of Evaluators
Elements.BodyText: Research shows that the optimal number of evaluators for HE is between three and five, as this range captures the best return on investment for problem discovery.
Elements.Notes: Nielsen's studies indicate that a single evaluator finds approximately 35% of problems, three evaluators find around 60%, and five evaluators find around 75%. Beyond five, each additional evaluator yields diminishing returns relative to cost.

Items.Text: A single evaluator finds only about one-third of all usability problems on average.
Three to five evaluators is the recommended range for maximum cost-effectiveness.
Each evaluator brings a unique perspective, collectively improving problem coverage.
Adding more than five evaluators yields rapidly diminishing returns on new findings.

Topics.Title: Severity Rating
Topics.Summary: Severity ratings allow evaluators to prioritize usability problems by estimating the impact of each violation on the user experience. This topic explains the standard severity scale and how to apply it consistently.

Elements.Title: Purpose of Severity Ratings
Elements.BodyText: Severity ratings help design and development teams prioritize which usability problems to fix first given limited time and resources.
Elements.Notes: Not all usability violations are equally harmful. A cosmetic inconsistency in button labeling warrants far less attention than a workflow that prevents task completion. Severity ratings make this prioritization explicit and defensible.

Items.Text: Severity ratings transform qualitative findings into a prioritized action list.
They help stakeholders make informed trade-off decisions about fix sequencing.
Ratings provide a shared language for communicating problem urgency across teams.

Elements.Title: Nielsen's Severity Rating Scale
Elements.BodyText: Nielsen's standard severity scale runs from 0 to 4, with 0 indicating no usability problem and 4 indicating a usability catastrophe that must be fixed before launch.
Elements.Notes: 0 = Not a usability problem. 1 = Cosmetic problem only — fix if time permits. 2 = Minor usability problem — low priority fix. 3 = Major usability problem — important to fix, high priority. 4 = Usability catastrophe — imperative to fix before product can be released.

Items.Text: A rating of 0 means the evaluator flagged a potential issue but it does not constitute an actual problem.
Ratings of 1 and 2 represent cosmetic and minor issues that should be addressed when resources allow.
A rating of 3 indicates a significant problem that meaningfully impairs task completion.
A rating of 4 represents a showstopper that prevents users from completing a primary task.

Elements.Title: Factors Influencing Severity
Elements.BodyText: Severity is determined by three key factors: the frequency with which the problem occurs, the impact it has on users, and the persistence of the problem across the interface.
Elements.Notes: A problem that appears on every page and completely blocks task completion is clearly severity 4. A problem that appears once in a rarely used section and causes only minor confusion is likely severity 1 or 2. Evaluators should consider all three factors before assigning a rating.

Items.Text: Frequency refers to how often users are expected to encounter the problem during normal use.
Impact refers to how severely the problem disrupts the user's ability to complete their task.
Persistence refers to whether the problem recurs or can be avoided after encountering it once.
A violation that is both frequent and high-impact will almost always receive a high severity rating.

Elements.Title: Assigning and Recording Ratings
Elements.BodyText: Each evaluator assigns severity ratings independently before any aggregation discussion to prevent anchoring and groupthink from distorting individual assessments.
Elements.Notes: When evaluators later compare ratings for the same problem, disagreements should prompt discussion rather than automatic averaging. Sometimes a disagreement reveals that two evaluators interpreted a problem differently, which itself is useful information.

Items.Text: Severity ratings must be assigned before evaluators share or compare findings.
Each rating should be justified with a brief rationale tied to frequency, impact, or persistence.
Rating disagreements between evaluators are opportunities to refine problem descriptions.
Final agreed ratings should be recorded alongside the problem description in the formal report.

Topics.Title: Aggregating Findings Across Evaluators
Topics.Summary: After individual evaluations are complete, findings must be systematically combined to create a single, deduplicated list of usability problems. This topic explains the aggregation process and how to resolve evaluator differences.

Elements.Title: Why Aggregation Is Necessary
Elements.BodyText: Because different evaluators identify different subsets of problems, combining findings from multiple evaluators produces a more complete and reliable picture of the interface's usability issues.
Elements.Notes: Aggregation is not simply merging lists — it requires careful deduplication and synthesis. Two evaluators may have found the same underlying problem but described it differently or attributed it to different heuristics.

Items.Text: Individual evaluators each find only a subset of the total usability problems present.
Aggregation maximizes problem coverage by combining the unique findings of each evaluator.
The aggregated list is the primary deliverable that informs design revision decisions.

Elements.Title: The Aggregation Meeting
Elements.BodyText: Evaluators come together in a structured meeting to present their findings, deduplicate overlapping issues, and negotiate final severity ratings for each problem.
Elements.Notes: A neutral facilitator should manage the aggregation meeting to ensure all evaluators contribute equally and that quieter evaluators' findings are not dismissed. The meeting should be time-boxed to maintain focus.

Items.Text: Each evaluator presents their complete findings list before group discussion begins.
Duplicate issues are identified and merged into a single consolidated finding.
Where evaluators disagree on severity, discussion should center on observable evidence.
The output is a single master list with agreed problem descriptions and severity ratings.

Elements.Title: Deduplication and Problem Merging
Elements.BodyText: Deduplication involves identifying problems that multiple evaluators reported and deciding whether they represent the same underlying issue or distinct but related problems.
Elements.Notes: A useful rule of thumb: if the same root cause and the same fix would resolve two reported issues, they should be merged. If they have different root causes or require different fixes, they should remain separate even if they appear superficially similar.

Items.Text: Compare problem descriptions carefully — similar symptoms may reflect different root causes.
Merge problems only when they share the same root cause and the same recommended fix.
Keep related but distinct problems separate to avoid obscuring important nuances in the findings.
Document which evaluators identified each problem to reflect breadth of discovery.

Elements.Title: Negotiating Severity Across Evaluators
Elements.BodyText: When evaluators assign different severity ratings to the same problem, the group must reach a consensus rating through evidence-based discussion.
Elements.Notes: Simply averaging ratings is not recommended because it can mask meaningful disagreements. If consensus cannot be reached, both the range and the reasoning should be documented. The highest defensible rating is often the safer choice to avoid understating risk.

Items.Text: Encourage evaluators to explain the reasoning behind their severity ratings before negotiating.
Consensus should be grounded in observable evidence, not personal preference.
Avoid simple mathematical averaging as it can produce ratings that no evaluator actually endorsed.
When consensus is impossible, document the range of ratings and the rationale for each position.

Topics.Title: Writing Formal Heuristic Evaluation Reports
Topics.Summary: The formal HE report is the primary deliverable that communicates findings to design teams and stakeholders. This topic outlines the structure, content requirements, and quality standards for professional HE reports.

Elements.Title: Report Structure and Components
Elements.BodyText: A well-structured HE report typically includes an executive summary, evaluation context, methodology description, consolidated findings table, and recommendations section.
Elements.Notes: The findings table is the centerpiece of the report. It should list each problem with its location, description, heuristic(s) violated, severity rating, and recommended fix. Organizing problems by severity (high to low) makes the report immediately actionable.

Items.Text: The executive summary provides a high-level overview for stakeholders who will not read the full report.
The methodology section documents who conducted the evaluation, when, and under what conditions.
Findings should be organized in a table sorted from highest to lowest severity.
Each finding entry should include location, description, heuristic, severity, and recommended fix.
A recommendations section may synthesize findings into broader design improvement themes.

Elements.Title: Writing Effective Problem Descriptions
Elements.BodyText: Problem descriptions must be precise, neutral, and specific enough that a designer can locate and understand the violation without having been part of the evaluation.
Elements.Notes: Avoid vague language such as 'the navigation is confusing.' Instead, specify: 'The secondary navigation menu disappears when a user scrolls past the hero image, providing no persistent access to sub-category pages (Heuristic 6: Recognition Over Recall).' Specificity is what makes a report actionable.

Items.Text: Describe the problem objectively without subjective or emotionally loaded language.
Specify the exact interface location — screen name, component, and interaction step.
Link each description explicitly to the heuristic it violates to support the finding's validity.
Avoid describing the desired solution in the problem description — keep problem and recommendation separate.

Elements.Title: Formulating Recommendations
Elements.BodyText: Recommendations translate each identified problem into actionable design guidance that the team can implement in the next iteration.
Elements.Notes: Recommendations should be practical and proportionate to the severity of the problem. A severity 4 problem warrants a detailed, prioritized recommendation. A severity 1 cosmetic issue may only need a brief suggestion. Avoid recommending wholesale redesigns for minor violations.

Items.Text: Each recommendation should directly address the root cause identified in the problem description.
Recommendations should be proportionate in scope to the severity of the problem.
Where possible, reference established patterns or conventions that address the violation.
Framing recommendations positively — what to do, not just what to avoid — is more useful to designers.

Elements.Title: Using Visual Evidence
Elements.BodyText: Annotated screenshots and screen recordings significantly increase the clarity and credibility of HE reports by providing direct visual evidence of each violation.
Elements.Notes: For each severity 3 or 4 finding, a supporting screenshot with annotation arrows or callouts is strongly recommended. Visual evidence reduces ambiguity about where the problem occurs and speeds up designer comprehension.

Items.Text: Screenshots should be captured at the moment the violation is most visible or impactful.
Annotations should clearly mark the specific element or area where the violation occurs.
Captions below images should connect the visual evidence explicitly to the problem description.
For interaction-based violations, short screen recordings may communicate the issue more effectively than static images.

Elements.Title: Report Quality Standards
Elements.BodyText: Professional HE reports must be clear, consistent, and credible — free of vague language, unsupported claims, and internal contradictions.
Elements.Notes: Before submitting a report, evaluators should review it against a quality checklist: Are all findings supported by a specific heuristic? Are severity ratings justified? Is language neutral and professional? Are recommendations actionable? Peer review of reports before submission improves quality significantly.

Items.Text: Every finding must be anchored to a specific Nielsen heuristic, not general design intuition.
Severity ratings must be accompanied by a brief justification referencing frequency, impact, or persistence.
Language throughout the report should remain neutral, professional, and free of speculation.
Recommendations must be feasible within the realistic constraints of the design project.

Topics.Title: Evaluating Peer Prototypes
Topics.Summary: This module requires students to apply the full HE process independently to three peer prototypes. This topic outlines the expectations, workflow, and professional conduct standards for peer prototype evaluations.

Elements.Title: Module Assignment Overview
Elements.BodyText: Each student independently evaluates three peer prototypes using Nielsen's ten heuristics, assigns severity ratings, and produces a formal HE report for each prototype evaluated.
Elements.Notes: The three-prototype requirement reflects the real-world practice of evaluating multiple design alternatives or iterative versions of a product. It also gives students practice calibrating their evaluation approach across different interface contexts.

Items.Text: Students evaluate three distinct peer prototypes independently, without collaboration during the evaluation phase.
A separate formal HE report must be produced for each prototype evaluated.
All ten Nielsen heuristics must be systematically considered during each evaluation.
Severity ratings must be applied to every documented finding using the standard 0–4 scale.

Elements.Title: Maintaining Evaluator Independence
Elements.BodyText: The independence requirement means students must complete their individual evaluations and draft reports before viewing or discussing findings with any other evaluator of the same prototype.
Elements.Notes: Independence prevents anchoring — the tendency to adjust one's own assessments to match those of a more vocal or credible peer. In professional practice, independence is what gives aggregated findings their validity.

Items.Text: Do not share or discuss findings with classmates until all individual evaluations are fully documented.
Record findings as you discover them — do not rely on memory to reconstruct observations later.
Independence ensures your report reflects your own expert assessment, not a group consensus.
Collaboration before completion of individual reports undermines the validity of the evaluation.

Elements.Title: Professional Conduct in Peer Evaluation
Elements.BodyText: Evaluating a peer's prototype requires maintaining a professional, constructive tone that focuses on interface design decisions rather than on the designer's choices or abilities.
Elements.Notes: Students may feel uncomfortable identifying problems in a classmate's work. Frame this as standard professional practice — all designs have usability issues, and identifying them is how design improves. Critique the interface, not the designer.

Items.Text: All findings must be framed objectively with reference to heuristics and observable evidence.
Avoid personal commentary about the prototype designer's skill, effort, or intent.
Constructive recommendations respect the designer's creative direction while addressing genuine violations.
Professional evaluators recognize that usability problems are a normal part of iterative design.

Elements.Title: Calibrating Evaluations Across Prototypes
Elements.BodyText: Applying a consistent standard across three different prototypes requires active calibration — evaluators must ensure they are not applying stricter or looser criteria as they progress through evaluations.
Elements.Notes: A common pitfall is that evaluators become fatigued by the third prototype and log fewer findings. Another pitfall is that evaluators unconsciously raise their bar after seeing a high-quality prototype. Returning to the heuristics as a checklist before each evaluation helps maintain consistency.

Items.Text: Use the same systematic walkthrough process for each prototype regardless of perceived quality.
Review all ten heuristics before beginning each new evaluation to reset your assessment frame.
Do not let the quality of one prototype unconsciously shift the standard applied to others.
A consistent number of walkthroughs per prototype helps control for evaluation depth variation.
